Comments of Mainspring Energy, Inc. on Co-Located Generation and Data Center 
Integration 
Dear Secretary Bose: 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 
385.211, Mainspring Energy, Inc. respectfully submits the attached comments in 
response to the Commission’s Order Instituting Proceeding issued on February 20, 
2025 and the subsequent filings by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. and other parties on 
March 24, 2025. 
Mainspring appreciates the Commission’s leadership in addressing the growing 
challenge of integrating large, high-load-factor customers such as data centers while 
maintaining grid reliability. We are a dispatchable generation technology provider 
actively developing co-located and behind-the-meter projects across the PJM footprint. 
In the attached comments, Mainspring: 
●​ Supports PJM’s exploration of new flexibility frameworks, including Options 6 and 
7;​
 
●​ Recommends preserving the two existing BTMG classes (retail and non-retail) 
while establishing a new tariff-defined class for repurposed legacy generation 
(Option 3);​
 
●​ Proposes specific tariff language to support this third class and improve 
transparency around cost allocation and interconnection study requirements;​

●​ Urges the Commission to require PJM to enhance forecasting by gathering 
relevant data on co-located generation; and​
 
●​ Encourages FERC and state regulators to continue aligning incentives for 
dispatchable, on-site capacity deployment to support reliability and customer 
affordability.​
 
We look forward to continued collaboration with the Commission, PJM, and 
stakeholders to advance resilient, affordable, and U.S.-engineered energy solutions. 
Respectfully submitted,​
  ​
 /s/ Brian Kauffman​
 Brian Kauffman​

COMMENTS OF MAINSPRING ENERGY, INC. REGARDING CO-LOCATED 
GENERATION AND DATA CENTER INTEGRATION  
Executive Summary 
The Utility-Data Center “seam” is bearing much of the brunt of tightening regional grid 
reserve margins and rising customer costs. Mainspring is providing solutions to utilities, large 
energy users and grid operators to rapidly bring new capacity. Mainspring’s Linear Generator 
can be configured as a new traditional grid-scale generator, new generators at retail customer 
sites behind the meter (BTMG), and non-retail BTMG deployed rapidly by public power entities. 
Other key takeaways:  
●​ Upon close review, PJM’s tariff is not just and reasonable because it lacks explicit details 
on how legacy generation can transition to become BTMG.  
●​ PJM’s detailed analysis of Option 3 describes a new class of BTMG. What PJM 
describes as Option 3 is not currently addressed in the tariff in a coherent fashion. This 
is a meaningful omission in the Tariff as many large generators are considering 
transitioning to this configuration to serve large loads. 
●​ In addition, we also respectfully urge the Commission to preserve the existing and 
historic BTMG classes for resources that enter service behind a customer’s meter 
(primarily under retail jurisdiction).  
●​ Next, we also recommend eliminating the cap on Non-Retail BTMG. 
●​ We offer detailed recommendations on black start, ancillary service and specifically, 
reserve cost allocation.

●​ After this, we explore implications to forecasting and request FERC to require PJM to 
gather information on customers with co-located generation to properly plan long-term 
and operationally. 
●​ Finally, we stand ready to work with states and all stakeholders to develop Options 6 and 
7 offered by PJM and other new flexibility solutions.  
Introduction 
Mainspring Energy is actively developing on-site and co-located projects in the PJM 
region and anticipates operating projects under one or more of the eight “Options” described in 
PJM’s March 24 Answer. We appreciate the vital work undertaken by the Commission, PJM, 
states, utilities and other stakeholders to incorporate large loads into the grid quickly while 
preserving reliability and minimizing cost. We are regularly speaking with customers across the 
country about the “seam” that requires creative solutions. The high load factor, data center - 
utility seam, is a major area of focus for us and Mainspring’s Linear Generator was built for this 
moment.  
PJM is up for this challenge. PJM has been a global leader at integrating large loads. 
However, new co-located generation is likely needed to manage the ramp in new loads over the 
next 5 to 10 years. As such, we are concerned that PJM’s comments and Tariff do not 
adequately distinguish the range of planning, markets and operational steps involved in 
re-purposing legacy, front of the meter PJM generation into behind the meter generation.  
The reliability challenge is indeed tremendous; PJM’s Board recently observed that, 
“Taking the anticipated 2025 load forecast into account, the PJM system could see a capacity 
shortage as soon as the 2026/27 Delivery Year.”1 As Mainspring describes in the enclosed 
whitepaper, Bring Your Own Power (BYOP), data center availability is low while demand for 
capacity is incredibly high, including in PJM’s footprint.2 PJM should not overlook the opportunity 
for help from new retail and non-retail generation to offset the growth in large loads. 
Data centers can not afford delays in interconnection. As we uncovered in the BYOP 
whitepaper, many new loads are receiving 3-5 year estimates for grid delivery of power. For a 
100 MW data center, three years of delay translates to over $500M in lost revenue. In response 
to these pressures and the need to protect other captive ratepayers, PJM and its member states 
should take extra effort to enable all forms of new generation: front of the meter PJM resources, 
retail resources at customer sites (BTMG), and non-retail BTMG deployed quickly by public 
power entities. We urge all stakeholders to think constructively about how new, dispatchable 
behind the meter generation can be expanded within today’s existing paradigms.  
PJM’s tariff is currently insufficient because it lacks details that explain the detailed 
process and costs to re-purpose legacy generation into behind the meter generation. The 
2 Whitepaper is also available on our website at https://www.mainspringenergy.com/byop/  
1 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2024/20241209-board-let
ter-outlining-action-on-capacity-market-adjustments-rri-and-sis.pdf  
3

Commission should correct this omission by requiring the rules that PJM describes under 
“Option 3” to be inserted into the Tariff as a new class of BTMG resources.  
Simultaneously, Mainspring agrees with PJM that it is time to prioritize enabling new 
frameworks that address the utility - data center seam. We are intrigued by PJM’s 
forward-looking proposals in Options 6 and 7. We are especially encouraged by PJM’s 
emphasis on “non-firm” grid service models aligned with on-site power. These opportunities, as 
PJM notes, depend on proactive state ratemaking to align customer incentives. The recent 
release of the first phase of Duke’s Rethinking Load Growth study in February 2025 provides a 
strong foundation, though significant work remains to translate these findings into actionable 
plans that support customer affordability and incentivize flexible development.3  
In summary, Mainspring’s analysis focused on Option 3 at this juncture concludes that 
the Tariff is not just and reasonable. In these comments, Mainspring highlights its rationale for 
why Option 3 requires Tariff additions, what those additions are, and provides support for PJM’s 
expeditious enablement of new Options 6 and 7, among other recommendations. 
Procedural Background 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, Mainspring submits these comments in 
response to the Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order Instituting Proceeding under Section 
206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other Proceedings (the “Show Cause 
Order”).4 In the Show Cause Order, the Commission specifically invited comment on these 
issues after the filings dated March 24, 2025 of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), the 
Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Public Service Gas & Electric, Allegheny Electric 
Cooperative, Inc., Silver Run Electric, LLC, Dayton Power and Light Company, and NextEra 
Energy Transmission MidAtlantic, Inc.  
Mainspring timely filed a doc-less motion to intervene on March 6, 2025 under EL25-49. 
Earlier, on December 9, 2024, Mainspring filed co-located generation post-technical comments 
under AD24-11.5  
About Mainspring 
Founded in 2010 by Stanford-trained engineers, Mainspring Energy is pioneering 
resilient, affordable, and clean generation technologies. Our flagship product, the Linear 
Generator, is the result of years of research into high-efficiency electricity generation and is now 
deployed across various sectors. With over 70 years of aggregated runtime and industry-leading 
uptime, our modular units deliver dispatchable power with flexible fuel options.  
Our customers include Lineage Logistics, Prologis, Kroger, and utilities such as AEP and 
Florida Power & Light. Mainspring joined the EPRI DCFlex initiative in January 2025, aimed at 
5 https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/filedownload?fileid=AB9D8BB7-268E-CC2A-991D-93AC32200000

demonstrating how data centers can stabilize the grid and improve interconnection. 
Mainspring’s small unit size enables five nines of uptime with minimal capacity overbuild.  
Solutions for Data Centers 
In 2025, Mainspring plans to construct several data center generation projects, including 
in a PJM state. We foresee implementing various configurations across these projects and 
emphasize that the Commission should preserve operational flexibility and opportunities for 
phased development.  
For instance, in Phase 1, we can deliver a power solution within 9 months to serve the 
data center as a prime power source. In Phase 2, once grid interconnection is feasible, 
configurations may vary: the linear generators could supplement the grid on a continuous basis 
(operating as “behind the meter generation” to PJM). Alternatively, in Phase 2 linear generators 
could be used only to manage peak on-site loads and/or grid peaks via an “interruptible 
program” (also as “behind the meter generation” to PJM). Or, as a third option in Phase 2, they 
could serve as full backup in a diesel-free “2N” configuration (again, to PJM this would classify 
as “behind the meter generation”).6  
In Phase 3, as cleaner fuels become more available, our generators can transition to 
biogas, green hydrogen, ammonia, or fuel blends—without major capital reinvestment. These 
phases are described in more detail in the enclosed 2024 whitepaper Bring Your Own Power 
(BYOP), co-authored by Stanford University Fellow, Susanna Kass, and Mainspring CEO 
Shannon Miller. Another option and phase could involve Mainspring’s units transitioning into 
PJM front of the meter capacity (such as under PJM Option 1 or 2).  
We underscore that a menu of options is critical. The prime concerns for data centers 
are speed and reliability, as we underscore in Figure 1, below. Data centers and other large 
users must have the ability to decide the fate of the generation that they are paying to bring to 
the grid, especially given the higher reliability requirements data centers face relative to 99% of 
other customers on the grid. 
A broad range of industry participants are increasingly focused on adding mechanisms 
for data center flexibility. Two of the most promising solutions are to (1) bring new, 
around-the-clock generation such that new demands do not put any new pressure on the grid 
and (2) run on-site generation for peaking (such as ~1,000 hours/year) non-emergency 
purposes to alleviate grid stress. Some U.S. utilities nationally are already developing programs 
that fit into this second category and align incentives for data centers to be flexible.7 As 
discussed, Mainspring’s solutions fit critical reliability needs.

Behind the Meter Generation (BTMG) 
Before making specific recommendations, we highlight key attributes of BTMG. First, 
BTMG is a suitable configuration moving ahead in line with PJM preferences. Grid limitations 
have led to growing reliance on “bridge to grid” models, where retail customers, in consultation 
with their local utility, bring their own capacity at least for Phase 1. Once the load customer is 
connected to PJM’s system, it becomes “network load” subject to the terms of the entity 
receiving transmission service. Therefore, the BTMG models should satisfy PJM’s stated 
preference for co-located configurations to retain the load as network load. That said, the 
concept of “network load” may need to evolve.  
Second, reducing customer demand has equivalent if not better results than adding 
formal PJM-qualified generation capacity. While PJM references “bring your own capacity” 
(Option 6) as formally qualified resources that add formal MWs on the supply side, adding 
BTMG reduces the demand on the PJM grid and can be done much faster. In addition, having 
more generation on the distribution system reduces transmission and distribution losses. 
Therefore, at Mainspring we think of BTMG as “bringing” new capacity, also.   
Two Separate BTMG Classes are in the PJM Tariff and Manuals Today: 
Retail and Non-Retail BTMG 
“BTMG” refers to customer-sited generation not registered as a wholesale PJM 
resource.8 PJM described BTMG in 2004 at a single customer site. Later, “this definition was 
subsequently expanded to permit inclusion of municipals and EDCs (“Non-Retail”) that use 
distribution facilities to serve loads, with the consent of the owners or lessee of the distribution 
facilities”.9 Mainspring agrees with PJM that these are in many important ways, separate 
constructs. There exists a large body of rules, captured under PJM Manual 14D that pertain only 
to Non-Retail Behind the Meter Generation.  
As such, why does PJM’s Answer often lump these two classes together into its 
Answer? PJM’s Answer often obscures their unique regulatory and operational characteristics. 
Any future analyses and reforms should more carefully distinguish between these two forms. 
Further, it is critical that PJM retain these classes of BTMG as separate from existing PJM 
generation, such as legacy nuclear units, that transition to become BTMG.  
A Third Class is Needed: Repurposed Generation Capacity into BTMG   
Much industry attention has focused on reassigning existing grid-connected capacity to 
large loads.PJM continues this trend in its Answer describing “Option 3”. As a company 
developing new, greenfield on-site generation, Option 3 looks foreign and clearly distinct from

Tariff Language Needed: Repurposed Generation Capacity into BTMG 
​
Clearly, repurposing existing assets to become behind the meter generation adds 
complexity, time and costs. Such steps should be available and transparent. These 
PJM-identified requirements described in PJM’s Answer under “Existing Option 3 “ should be 
added to the PJM Tariff given their importance to all market participants. The Commission 
should require PJM to add this tariff language describing this list of required studies and 
approaches to allocate study and interconnection upgrade costs appropriately for this class of 
existing generation repurposed into BTMG.    
Recommended Language: 
●​ Definition. Repurposed Behind the Meter Generation (BTMG) is generation that is 
located behind a retail customer meter that was previously a Generation Capacity 
Resource. 
●​ Study Process for Becoming a Repurposed BTMG. The process is multi-staged and 
includes the following phases10: 
○​ Complete Transmission Owner retail load integration study, 
○​ Present solutions at the Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee 
(traditionally, Supplemental Projects), 
○​ PJM will perform a “Do No Harm Study” to evaluate how a Supplemental Project 
will impact the reliability of the Transmission System.  
■​ If as a result of the do no harm study, system upgrades are found to be 
required such upgrades will be considered part of the Supplemental 
Project and are the responsibility of the Transmission Owner sponsoring 
the Supplemental Project 
■​ Supplemental Projects are cost allocated to the local Transmission 
Owner’s zone pursuant to individual Transmission Owner cost allocation 
frameworks, 
○​ The generation owner will request a “Necessary Study” to change the 
interconnection.  
■​ PJM will conduct a Necessary Study 
■​ Transmission Owners review PJM’s study analysis to verify that analysis 
and/or perform additional transmission owner analysis pursuant to their 
processes or requirements 
○​ An aggregation of large load additions could trigger regional (as opposed to local) 
transmission system needs, which would be identified as part of the Regional 
Transmission Expansion Planning process in Schedule 6 of the Operating 
Agreement. 
■​ That load could rise to regional RTEP needs when determined during the 
annual load forecasting process in collaboration with LSEs 
■​ With the updated load forecast, the RTEP process may incorporate the 
impact of the transition of the Generation Capacity Resource. 
10 Adopted from PJM Answer, pp 6-8 
8

●​ Cost Allocation for Interconnection Upgrades. The following costs may be required when 
Generation Capacity Resources become Repurposed BTMG. 
○​ Supplemental projects pursuant to local TO methodology 
○​ RTEP upgrades pursuant to RTEP cost allocation 
○​ Generator interconnection for the changes to its facility to accommodate the load 
 
Black Start and Ancillary Services Cost Allocation  
Indeed, proper cost allocation is critical. To that point, we also highlight PJM’s assertion 
on page 36 that all co-located data center configurations “appear to require” grid ancillary 
services and black start. To PJM’s credit, the RTO acknowledges that this conclusion is  
uncertain. In our experience, technology matters: linear generators, unlike nuclear units, can 
provide their own ancillary services and black start capabilities for on-site loads. Most likely, 
behind the meter generation configurations with nuclear units will desire to leverage grid 
services differently than those configurations with linear generators.  
For a hypothetical situation, imagine a 200 MW data center. The data center is served 
100 MW from standard grid power and 100 MW with MW BTMG nuclear generation. 
Operationally, the data center is sized for 200 MW interconnection to the PJM system but only 
uses 100 MW at 99% of the time. Charging customers for grid services the 1% of the time 
needed to supplement the 100 MW co-located generation is appropriate when those services 
are necessary. In addition, from a planning perspective, the customer has already secured 
sufficiently sized interconnection to supplement its nuclear generation on-site, so that cost issue 
has already been addressed.  
 
Reserves Cost Allocation 
PJM also erroneously suggests that all load with BTMG requires the use of PJM 
reserves above a reasonable threshold. In other words, PJM suggests if  the customer is 
generally receiving 100 MW of service from PJM and 100 MW from behind the meter 
generation, the customer should actually be paying for more than only 100 MW of reserves.  
This issue is nuanced and the answer changes with the exact scenario. Configurations 
could be designed to entirely avoid relying on reserves for the extra 100 MW. For instance, 
some loads are incredibly flexible and could drop immediately with the loss of on-site 
generation. 
Further, the interconnection could be sized appropriately for this situation. A 200 MW 
data center with a 100 MW load interconnection (and 100 MW BTMG) is different from a 200 
MW data center with a 200 MW load interconnection (also with 100 MW BTMG). In the first 
case, only 100 MW could ever flow from the grid to the customer. Whereas in the second case, 
the customer could technically draw upon 200 MW if controls were not in place.   
9

Mainspring acknowledges that reforms may be needed to ensure BTMG benefits extend 
beyond long-term resource adequacy to system reliability needs in real-time. Activities in the 
current PJM Reserve Certainty Senior Task Force are proof that navigating this won’t be 
easy.Transitions in data center loads are generally speaking, increasingly impactful to the grid.11 
However, this reserves issue does not appear to require urgent resolution and is likely better 
handled through PJM’s stakeholder process. 
 
Non-Retail BTMG Cap Should be Lifted 
​
Public power entities have a unique opportunity to move quickly to develop to site and 
build new generation and implement new customer tariffs to address the “seam”. The Non-Retail 
BTMG model allows public power to operate generation on the distribution system, rather than 
only behind an individual customer meter. Therefore, we encourage public power entities to 
leverage the Non-Retail BTMG pathway to introduce new generation quickly to the system. 
 
Mainspring knows first-hand the advantages of public power entities to solve this 
problem. Mainspring has been contracted by a public power entity to deliver 36 MW of 
generation on the distribution system to offset new build of a data center. While the project is 
outside of PJM, many of the same lessons apply. We are eager to bring our experience to the 
municipal and cooperative utilities in the PJM footprint.  
 
PJM’s Answer emphasizes that innovation may be needed in the Non-Retail BTMG 
space. Mainspring acknowledges that certain elements of the Non-Retail BTMG framework 
should also be re-examined such as the fact that these resources “do not carry reserves equal 
to the installed reserve margin”.12 Any further action should also appreciate the potential for 
expansion of Non-Retail BTMG, given the tremendous promise of this model to solve the 
capacity gap quickly. The current limit poses a risk to the grid by limiting the amount of new 
capacity available to add to the system. The Commission should ask PJM to lift the cap on 
Non-Retail BTMG above the current 3 GW limit.  
Support for Exploring Options 6 and 7 
Mainspring strongly supports further exploration of Options 6 and 7, recognizing the 
potential of each to offer complementary pathways for integrating large loads. However, these 
are not yet viable alternatives for near-term deployment. BTMG remains the most reliable 
near-term solution and should be welcomed as “bridge to grid” pathways, capable of maturing 
into, and working alongside Options 6 or 7. 
Option 6 appears best suited to a range of use cases, from baseload or prime power use 
cases to peaking; Option 7 to intermediate applications; and Option 8 to peaking needs. Each 
faces emissions limitations, which low-emission technology like Mainspring’s can help navigate.

Detailed Observations 
Option 6 – Bring Your Own Capacity (BYOC) 
●​ We are intrigued by this model, where customer-owned generation becomes a 
PJM resource serving both system needs and the load.  
●​ However, PJM’s reluctance to create an expedited interconnection path for 
co-located generation is one reason among others that customers may default to 
BTMG.  
Option 7 – Interruptible Service 
●​ Mainspring supports non-capacity backed service models in which loads can 
self-supply or curtail in exchange for avoided capacity and transmission charges.  
●​ PJM should explore whether a new “non-firm” load category is needed in its 
planning models, as current frameworks do not account for this at the 
transmission level. 
Option 8 – Demand Response with Diesel Gensets 
●​ We agree on the value of generation-based demand response but caution that 
diesel units are unsuitable for long run times. This approach faces regulatory 
uncertainty and concerns over local air quality impacts.  
●​ PJM should instead throw its weight behind preparing for the future. As 
discussed in the enclosed BYOP whitepaper, “we need to examine if the concept 
of primary and backup systems is sustainable, in comparison to a resilient 
system that can operate as both”. 
●​ Linear generators are better suited due to lower emissions and longer runtime 
capabilities, and they allow for larger installations without breaching emissions 
limits. Mainspring’s Linear generator produces 97% fewer nitrous oxides than a 
typical diesel generator.  
Forecasting Needs 
PJM’s load forecasting processes are robust but must evolve to integrate customer 
flexibility, including the ability to help local utilities and end-use customers to ascertain the 
financial value of accepting non-firm service. Specifically, PJM in concert with utilities, should 
allow customers to compare costs and time horizons for powering large loads.  
Customers should be able to compare a range of wired and on-site generation solutions 
prior to committing to a final infrastructure build. This has important implications to other rate 
classes, as well, who may be saddled with the costs of infrastructure for decades into the future. 
Further, large loads should be equipped to communicate evolving data center build phases and 
operations to PJM in real time.   
11

Conclusion: Mainspring’s Linear Generator and Key 
Recommendations to the Commission  
As PJM faces rising loads and tightening reserves, flexible technologies are critical. 
Mainspring’s Linear Generator offers: 
• Rapid Deployment: Modular, scalable, and available now. 
• Operational Flexibility: Reliable 24/7 operation with load-following. 
• Fuel Agility: Ready for natural gas, hydrogen, biogas, propane, and ammonia. 
• Environmental Leadership: Substantial emissions reductions. 
• Resilience: Redundant design and multiple fuel pathways. 
We urge the Commission to affirm the reliability value of new retail and non-retail behind 
the meter generation and require PJM to file tariff language that clarifies the rules around 
“transitioned” or “repurposed” legacy generation into BTMG generation (Option 3). We support 
PJM’s exploration of Options 6–7. We also encourage states to pursue policies enabling local, 
dispatchable generation for large loads. These tools will help ensure that the region remains a 
global leader in digital infrastructure and grid reliability at least cost. 
Mainspring is ready to collaborate with stakeholders to deliver on these goals. For further 
information, please contact RTO/FERC lead:
